Disquieted
dis-KWY-e-ted
v. (past part.)
From dis- (privative) and quiet, Latin quies, rest. Webster 1828: made uneasy or restless; disturbed; harassed. The word describes not agony but the loss of rest — a soul that cannot settle.

Biblical Definition

Disquieted is the psalmist’s word for a soul that will not settle, and Scripture puts it three times in the mouth of a believer questioning himself. Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance (Psalm 42:5), repeated at Psalm 42:11 and again at Psalm 43:5 as the refrain of two psalms. The structure is worth noting carefully: the man does not deny that he is disquieted, and he does not wait for the feeling to lift. He interrogates his own soul, refuses its verdict, and preaches to it — hope thou in God — on the ground of a future certainty, I shall yet praise him. That is the biblical handling of a downcast spirit, and it is neither denial nor surrender. The word also has an accusing use. Of the man who spends his life accumulating, the psalm says: Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them (Psalm 39:6). Here the disquiet is self-inflicted and pointless — a restless getting for an heir the getter cannot name.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DISQUIETED as made uneasy or restless; disturbed; harassed; deprived of peace or tranquillity of mind.

expand to see more

DISQUIETED, pp. — Made uneasy or restless; disturbed; deprived of quiet or tranquillity.

Harassed; vexed; agitated by care, fear, or trouble.

Applied to the mind or soul, denoting the loss of settled rest rather than acute pain.

Also applied to nations and to households in a state of unrest.

From dis-, apart or away, and Latin quies, rest — the root also of quiet, quiescent, and acquiesce.

Key Scripture

Psalm 42:5 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him for the help of his countenance."

Psalm 42:11 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

Psalm 43:5 — "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God."

Psalm 39:6 — "Surely every man walketh in a vain shew: surely they are disquieted in vain: he heapeth up riches, and knoweth not who shall gather them."

Modern Corruption

The therapeutic account of a downcast spirit asks the sufferer to sit with the feeling and validate it, where the psalmist questions his own soul, contradicts it, and preaches a future certainty to it.

expand to see more

Psalm 42 is the model, and its method is unfashionable in two directions at once. It does not suppress: the psalmist admits that his tears have been his meat day and night, that deep calls to deep, that all God’s waves have gone over him. But it does not indulge either. He turns and addresses himself in the second person — Why art thou cast down, O my soul? — and refuses to accept the soul’s account of the situation as final. Martyn Lloyd-Jones built his Spiritual Depression on exactly this observation: most of our unhappiness comes from listening to ourselves instead of talking to ourselves. The remedy prescribed is not a feeling but a fact, held in the future tense: I shall yet praise him.

The dictionary is not indifferent to real affliction, and this psalm forbids indifference. The man is genuinely in the land of Jordan, remembering better days at the house of God with a multitude, and taunted with Where is thy God? Scripture gives such a man permission to say all of it. What it does not give is permission to conclude from his condition that God has changed, and it supplies the discipline of self-address as the ordinary means of resistance. Psalm 39:6 adds the other warning: much of what people call anxiety is the disquiet of accumulation — restless getting for heirs one cannot name — and that species is cured by repentance rather than comfort.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hamah (H1993), to murmur, to be in tumult, to be disquieted; shachach (H7817), to be bowed down; ragaz (H7264), to tremble, to be agitated; Greek tarasso (G5015), to trouble, to stir up.

expand to see more

Hebrew hamah (H1993) — to murmur, roar, be in commotion; why art thou disquieted in me? (Psalm 42:5).

Hebrew shachach (H7817) — to be bowed down, to sink; the companion verb, rendered cast down.

Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to quiver, to be agitated; surely they are disquieted in vain (Psalm 39:6).

Greek tarasso (G5015) — to agitate, to trouble; Let not your heart be troubled (John 14:1).

Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious, to be divided in mind; Take no thought for your life (Matthew 6:25).

Usage

"Why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God (Psalm 42:5) — the soul questioned and then preached to."

"I shall yet praise him (Psalm 42:11) — a future certainty held against a present feeling."

"Surely they are disquieted in vain (Psalm 39:6) — restless getting for an heir the getter cannot name."
